endorsements.quote: AI models should be continuously monitored and stress-tested across different demographic subpopulations to detect and correct emerging biases.

Regulators and healthcare institutions should require AI companies to document bias mitigation efforts, disclose demographic performance metrics, and undergo independent third-party audits before clinical deployment.
Independent validations by external researchers or institutions can further ensure that model performance and fairness claims hold up under diverse, real-world conditions.
AI models must be trained on balanced datasets that represent a wide range of racial, ethnic, gender, and socioeconomic groups.
First, developers and healthcare institutions should actively collaborate with diverse communities to ensure AI systems reflect real-world patient diversity.

Developers can incorporate algorithmic fairness strategies, such as reweighting training samples, adversarial debiasing, and differential model tuning, to mitigate biases before deployment [ 56 , 57 ].

Another promising approach involves developing structured documentation protocols—akin to model “nutrition labels”—that summarize the model’s data sources, training methodology, known limitations, and prior performance across diverse patient populations [ 82 ].

Formalizing accountability encourages ongoing stakeholder engagement—patients, clinicians, policymakers, and developers—thereby strengthening public trust and reducing the risk of a loss of confidence that could hinder AI adoption in healthcare.

unlisted_practices: Establish harmonized global standards and international cooperation for healthcare AI regulation and cross-border data sharing.
Regulators should adopt adaptive, iterative oversight requiring periodic re-certification or ongoing post-deployment performance evaluation of AI systems.
Regulators should require eco-impact assessments and prioritize energy-efficient algorithms and renewable computing power for healthcare AI.
Adopt procurement policies that prioritize sustainable AI vendors.
Use hybrid or rule-based AI when interpretability is paramount, matching the AI category to the clinical task.
Define measurable transparency metrics such as explainability scores and the percentage of outputs accompanied by interpretable explanations.
Establish joint training programs and multidisciplinary working groups across AI developers, clinicians, policymakers and ethicists.
Retrain and upskill healthcare workers for AI-enhanced roles.
Embed ethical principles at the inception of model development through ethical-by-design guidelines and continuous impact assessments.
Publicly report model performance and bias audits.

screen.reason: The paper provides a multidisciplinary governance and oversight framework (the Regulatory Genome) and actionable ethical recommendations based on a structured literature review.
